conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my face and neck have been swelling up over the last three days. It’s really tender, and I can’t lie flat because I feel short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever or trouble swallowing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had fevers up to 102. But I can swallow fine. Just drooling a bit at night, which is weird.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We did a CT scan and it shows your parotid glands are enlarged on both sides, but no abscess. ENT thinks it’s sialadenitis—swelling of the salivary glands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I couldn’t breathe well after the CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re admitting you to the ICU tonight. We’re concerned about airway swelling. You got steroids and epinephrine, which helped. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My leg wound is okay, but it’s oozing a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have wound care look at it. For now, we’re focused on your neck. Your white count is up and lactate is elevated, so we started antibiotics just in case there’s infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without any breathing issues. That’s a big relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel a bit better. Still swollen, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending tests for viruses like mumps, EBV, and CMV. Your mumps IgG is positive, so you’ve had it before. IgM is pending—could mean a reactivation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was vaccinated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were, but immunity can wane. We’re also checking for fungal and bacterial causes. We’ll keep you on IV antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative. No bacteria growing. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a bloodstream one. But your parotid glands are still inflamed. ENT and Infectious Disease think it could be viral or related to your psoriatic arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EBV and CMV tests came back negative. No sign of those viruses. Mumps IgM is still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the rash on my chest? It showed up after the IV steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dermatology saw you. They think it’s pustular psoriasis, which can flare after high-dose steroids. We’re starting a strong topical cream—clobetasol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should improve. We’ll keep the cream going until your dermatology follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to transfer you to the regular floor today. Your breathing is stable, and you’re off oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I use my CPAP again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your face is still too swollen. We’ll try it later. For now, we’ll monitor you at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR was high when you came in—4.8—so we held your warfarin. It’s now 1.7, so we restarted it at a higher dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take 6 mg at home. Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started at 10 mg to get you therapeutic faster, but we’ll adjust based on tomorrow’s INR. Goal is around 2 to 3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line so you can get IV antibiotics at home if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my other conditions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s standard. We’ll make sure it’s positioned correctly with a chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray showed the PICC tip was too far—it was in the right atrium. We pulled it back. Now it’s in the right spot in the SVC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be, long-term. But we caught it quickly. You’re fine now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your skin scraping showed Trichophyton—fungal infection, probably ringworm on your arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know I had that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common. We’ll keep the antifungal cream you’re already on—miconazole. It should clear up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lactate is normal now—down from 5. That means your body is handling oxygen better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But you never had a fever, so we think it was from inflammation. It’s improving with treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.7—perfect. We’re lowering your warfarin to 4 mg daily, which is less than your home dose, but safer for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll check it at home and call my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Also, we’re switching you from IV to oral antibiotics—just a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ENT re-evaluated you. They don’t think this is a bacterial infection. More likely inflammation from your psoriatic arthritis or a viral cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started them because we couldn’t rule out infection. But now that you’re improving, we’ll stop them soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Swelling is less, and your labs are stable. We’re stopping the IV antibiotics today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow. We want to make sure your INR stays stable and you’re eating and breathing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started you on Bactrim daily. Since you’re on chronic steroids, you need protection against a lung infection called PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. Is it necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ID recommends it. Steroids lower your immunity, so this is a safety measure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mumps IgM came back pending—still no result. Until we know, avoid kids, pregnant women, and anyone with cystic fibrosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My family is vaccinated. Should I still worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Better safe. We’ll follow up with the state lab. For now, just be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you tomorrow. You’re breathing well, swelling is down, and labs are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care says it’s healing. Keep it clean and watch for redness or increased drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary. Follow up with ID, ENT, and your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if you have trouble breathing, fever, or the rash worsens. And get those outpatient labs done—LDH and liver tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Have a good one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep using your CPAP as tolerated. Even if it’s uncomfortable, try to use it part of the night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll build up slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And keep checking your INR. Call your doctor with the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got a home monitor. I’ll stay on top of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That helps a lot. Any other questions before you leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Everything’s clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Rest up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.
